title: Guide to Medicare Enrollment Periods
metaDescription: Learn the Medicare enrollment periods, including the initial 7-month window, the general enrollment period, and rules for employer coverage.
cardBlurb: When to sign up for Medicare across the initial, general, and special enrollment periods.
introText:
You can sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period, which lasts for 7 months, starting 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ending 3 months after the month you turn 65. At ModernWallet, we treat this signup window as a fixed date to confirm before making other retirement choices. Your coverage start date depends on the month you enroll.

If you miss that initial window, the General Enrollment Period runs from January 1 to March 31 each year. If you have employer group health coverage, a Special Enrollment Period lasts for 8 months after your coverage or employment ends.

sections.heading: The Initial Enrollment Period
sections.body:
Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts for 7 months, starting 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ending 3 months after the month you turn 65. This window is your first opportunity to sign up for Medicare. The exact day your coverage starts depends on the month you enroll.

Enrolling during the first 3 months provides coverage starting as early as the month you turn 65. If you enroll during the month you turn 65 or the 3 months after, your coverage start date still depends on the month you enroll. You can verify your specific coverage start date directly at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start).

The 7-month calendar count is fixed to the month you turn 65. If you turn 65 in June, the window begins March 1 and ends September 30. Anyone approaching age 65 can map their personal 7-month window based on their birth month.

sections.heading: The General Enrollment Period
sections.body:
The General Enrollment Period runs from January 1 to March 31 each year. This annual window allows individuals who missed their initial opportunity to sign up for Medicare. Coverage starts the month after you sign up.

If you enroll on January 15, your coverage begins on February 1. If you submit your enrollment in March, your coverage begins on April 1. Signing up during this period means waiting until the following month for your protection to begin.

You can confirm enrollment processing details online at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start). If you also compare coverage models, you can read our guide on [Medicare vs Medicare Advantage](/compare/medicare-vs-medicare-advantage/) to review plan types.

sections.heading: Rules for Medicare Enrollment Periods with Employer Coverage
sections.body:
The Special Enrollment Period for employer group health plan coverage ends 8 months after the group health plan coverage or the employment ends, whichever happens first. This window applies to individuals with health coverage through current employment.

The 8-month clock starts on the date employment ends or the date group health plan coverage ends, whichever comes first. If your job ends in April but your group plan coverage continues through May, the 8-month window begins in April. Confirm the exact status of your group coverage with your benefits administrator.

Other coverage types do not change this standard 8-month deadline. For questions about how COBRA or retiree plans work with this timeframe, check the rules at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start). You can also evaluate private supplement options in our guide on [Medicare Advantage vs Medigap](/compare/medicare-advantage-vs-medigap/).

sections.heading: What Late Enrollment Costs
sections.body:
If you wait to sign up when you must pay for Part B, you may pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B, and it goes up the longer you wait. This extra amount is added directly to your monthly premium bill.

According to [CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2026-medicare-parts-b-premiums-deductibles), the standard Part B premium is $202.90 each month. A late enrollment penalty increases this monthly cost. Because the penalty lasts for as long as you maintain Part B coverage, delaying enrollment produces an ongoing expense.

You can review detailed cost calculations in our guide to [Medicare costs and Part B premiums](/guides/medicare-costs-2026-part-b-premium-irmaa/). For individuals with lower income, state assistance programs may provide help, as outlined in our comparison of [Medicare vs Medicaid](/compare/medicare-vs-medicaid/).

sections.heading: Retiring Before 65 vs After 65
sections.body:
Leaving work before age 65 requires maintaining health coverage until your Medicare enrollment periods open at age 65. If you leave work early, you must arrange bridge coverage to protect your health and finances. Read our guide on [health insurance before Medicare in early retirement](/guides/health-insurance-before-medicare-early-retirement/) to explore options for covering those gap years.

Retiring after age 65 allows you to transition directly from employer group health plan coverage to Medicare using the Special Enrollment Period. That 8-month period begins as soon as either your employment or group health coverage ends. If you are coordinating this transition with retirement planning, see our guide on [how to retire at 67](/guides/how-to-retire-at-67/).

Ask HealthCare.gov how premium tax credits and your income estimate apply to you. You can also estimate your retirement cash flow with our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/).

sections.heading: A Timeline Checklist for Medicare Enrollment Periods
sections.body:
Tracking each deadline helps you avoid gaps in coverage and late fees across Medicare enrollment periods. You can organize your timeline around the dates established in federal rules.

- **Age 64 and 9 months.** Identify the start of your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, which begins 3 months before the month you turn 65.
- **Age 65.** Submit your enrollment during the month you turn 65 or within the 3 months prior to secure coverage starting as early as possible.
- **Age 65 and 3 months.** Note the end of your Initial Enrollment Period.
- **January 1 to March 31.** Use the General Enrollment Period if you missed your initial window, with coverage beginning the month after signup.
- **Leaving employment.** Note the 8-month Special Enrollment Period that begins when employment or group coverage ends, whichever comes first.

Confirm your exact dates on [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start) as your next step to prepare for your Medicare enrollment periods.

This page provides general educational information about Medicare enrollment rules and deadlines. It does not provide individualized legal, tax, financial, or health insurance advice. Consult a licensed insurance agent, certified public accountant, or financial advisor regarding your personal situation.

faqs.question: How long is the Medicare initial enrollment period?
faqs.answer: The Initial Enrollment Period lasts for 7 months. It begins 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after the month you turn 65. Your coverage start date depends on the month you enroll.

faqs.question: When does Medicare coverage start after you sign up in the General Enrollment Period?
faqs.answer: Coverage starts the month after you sign up during the General Enrollment Period. The General Enrollment Period runs from January 1 to March 31 each year.

faqs.question: How long do you have to sign up for Medicare after leaving a job?
faqs.answer: You have 8 months under the Special Enrollment Period for employer group health plan coverage. This 8-month window ends 8 months after your group health plan coverage or your employment ends, whichever happens first.

faqs.question: Is there a penalty for signing up late?
faqs.answer: If you wait to sign up when you must pay for Part B, you may pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B, and it goes up the longer you wait.

faqs.question: Do COBRA or retiree plans extend the Special Enrollment Period?
faqs.answer: They do not automatically extend the window. The Special Enrollment Period for employer coverage ends 8 months after employment or group health plan coverage ends, whichever happens first. Check the exact rules for your plan at [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start).

faqs.question: What is the standard Part B premium?
faqs.answer: The standard Part B monthly premium is $202.90, according to [CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2026-medicare-parts-b-premiums-deductibles). If you face a late enrollment penalty, that penalty is added to your monthly Part B payment.
